metadata.title: Roger Deakins looks at the lighting of scenes in Prisoners
metadata.description: Roger Deakins looks at the lighting of scenes in the movie Prisoners and discusses his approach, using still frames and lighting diagrams to illustrate.

content_html:
Prisoners – Alcon Entertainment

 

PRISONERS 1
Looking at Lighting

 

THE REST STOP

As originally scripted for ‘Prisoners’, this location was defined as a highway rest stop rather than as a brightly lit gas station. In the film ‘Revolutionary Road’ there had been a night scene set at a similar location and, although the content was very different, it gave me second thoughts about this ‘rest stop’ and where Loki would discover the parked RV. For ‘Revolutionary Road’ I had rigged three fluorescent-style streetlamps, that both appeared in shot and acted as my main source of light for the scene, and I would now require something of a similar nature. But I felt this present scene needed something more defined, a pool of light surrounded by darkness rather than a series of individual sources, with the suspect’s RV being parked to one side in the shadows. As I searched for inspiration online, a picture of a small rural gas station seemed to offer the perfect look so, with this image as a reference, I discussed the idea with Denis. I remember he liked the idea of the pool of light but was concerned that the RV would be in the shadows and that it was, as scripted, close to a wooded area. We had already looked at numerous roadside locations in the immediate Atlanta area but had seen none that had the necessary ingredients for our story. The gas station would be a new ask for our location scouts along with a need to fit this night shoot, which wasn’t a full day’s work, with something else that could be shot within a reasonable travel distance. The location also had to be such that we could close off the road when we were shooting and accommodate the large construction cranes that would be necessary to create our effects rain over a large area. The gas station that we chose is a little larger than the ideal that Denis or I had imagined but the large parking area and the woodland close by made it the only real option available. By bringing in some trees our production designer, Patrice Vermette, was able to close down the on-camera parking area, whilst a second parking area to the back of the gas station was a definite plus for our effects team, who had the task of making the rainstorm. Although the location was a little more distant than we would have liked I could argue that, if our pre rig crew could work there during the day, we would be ready to shoot as soon as it was fully dark, which would make up a considerable amount of time.

The rest stop lighting and action schematic


 

The RV is stopped under the trees


 

You can see from the schematic above that there was very little lighting necessary at this location. We did change out some of the mercury vapor lamps above the pumps, which were old and had become discolored, and we also added some florescent strips to the side of the store. On the billboard, we rigged a series of 400-watt Joker HMI lamps to down light the structure and we added two 1.2 HMIs to this same framework, which would act as a backlight for the rain seen in the camera angle that is looking back towards the gas station from behind the RV. As for most of our shooting of ‘Prisoners’, I had a rough sketch of the way Denis intended to stage each individual scene, whilst for some we had fully drawn storyboards.

THE BIRCH HOUSE

The Birch House at night


 

The Birch House lighting sketch


 

We chose a suburban development outside of Atlanta as the basis for the neighborhood that forms a key setting in the story of ‘Prisoners’ and we chose specific houses for the Birch family and the Dover family within walking distance of each other. We had a large amount of night work but, as much of it took place within this one primary location, I could pre light many of the individual areas in which we were shooting at the end of a previous day’s work. At no point did I want to use a ‘moonlight’ source, so everything I did was based on the use of practical lights that could appear in camera. Some of these sources were chosen in collaboration with the art department and others were simply ‘gag’ lights and bare bulbs of various sorts. Outside the Birch house, the trees were lit using MR16s and ‘mushroom’ bulbs, which were wrapped with blackwrap. The art department added specific practical lamps to each side of the front door and to the posts at the foot of the driveway. Behind the house I placed as series of 2K Blondes, probably a few more than the three that are specified in the sketch, to up light the trees and define the dark roofline as seen from the front of the house.

Pic 6 Viola Davis and Terrence Howard, inside the car


 

I remember talking to Patrice about the garage and the fact that it was white. There was the possibility of painting it down but, knowing there was a scene between Viola Davis and Terrence Howard as they sat in their car outside the house, I felt the white would work to my advantage if this scene could be staged in the driveway. During prep, I scouted for houses that had their Christmas lights up and used photographic references of these for discussions with Patrice as to what felt right in our neighborhood.

Franklin Birch walks home


 

To the right of the Birch House


 

As Franklin walks towards the Birch house and the candlelit vigil that is being held outside, I use a 2’ diameter, hand-held ring light to bring some warm light into Terrence’s face. This ring carried 6 or 7 x 40-watt household globes, dimmed down to contrast, what was the warmth of the candlelight, with the mix of the background florescent fixtures, car headlamps, etc.

Jake watches the vigil at the Birch House


 

Over Jake


 

The reverse from the Birch House looking towards the fleeing suspect


 

I will always do a sketch of the lighting I am thinking of as it gives me a concrete reference when talking with my gaffer, who was in this case Chris Napolitano with whom I have worked on numerous occasions. We would discuss the placement of each light as well as what the best unit for the particular job might be, after which Chris would organize the scheduling of this work with his rigging gaffer. For some, if not most, of the sets Chris and I would re visit them with the rigging team so that we would all be in sync. Whilst we were on a day shooting schedule, we would view the progress of this pre rigging for an hour or two at wrap, gradually filling in the background lighting for all our night work. To work with just two or three rigging electricians can be very efficient as it allows me to study the results before things go too far and make adjustments if necessary. By the time we came to shoot our night work on this location, most of the time-consuming lighting had been done and I could be more focused on what was happening in front of the camera.

THE BIRCH HOUSE INTERIOR

Birch House interior


 

Birch House interior plan


 

The interior of the Birch House was extremely small, so my lighting needed to come from practical sources that would appear in shot. Each lamp fixture was chosen with this in mind and the only interior light that I used, other than those that are seen, was a twin socket that held two 60-watt globes and was hidden behind the ceiling light in the front room. As we were shooting during the winter, it was hubris to expect a constant natural daylight outside the windows so the set dresser and I decided shear curtains would help to disguise the artificiality of the lighting I would use to replicate the daylight. To the front of the house there was little space to light in, so I used bounce sources close to the window. To the back of the house there was a large covered porch and it made more sense to use direct light, softened by a double layer of diffusion. To balance the color of the HMIs outside with the warmth of the interior, I used a ¼ or a ½ CTB on the glass of the windows rather than on the lamps. The gel was mounted on frames that fit each window so I could easily exchange a ¼ with a ½ or add one to another. Being away from the heat of the lamps this also meant the gel held its color for the whole of a shooting day as opposed to burning out if on the barn doors. We also dedicated a crane for a fly swat, which we used to cut out any sunlight that would affect the set interior. As Denis and I wanted the film to be shot in overcast, the interior sets were often held as weather cover for our exterior work, which meant that we would, more likely than not, be shooting inside when the sun was shining. In the same way as the night work, Chris and I would pre light the daylight interiors in advance of shooting, which was especially important if we were to move inside at any time for weather cover.

THE DOVER HOUSE EXT.

The back of the Dover House


 

The Dover house lighting sketch


 

I used a similar strategy to light the exterior of the Dover House as I had for the Birch House. For the back stair of the house I simply used a household socket above the door and a 75-watt mushroom bulb to focus the light down onto the deck area. Apart from the second low wattage practical by the window and a 2K Blond raking up the trees beyond, that is all the lighting used for this angle. Like almost all the night work in ‘Prisoners’, this shot would have been made at between 1.4 and 2.0 on a Master Prime lens.

THE DOVER HOUSE INT.

Loki and Mrs. Dover


 

Loki


 

Mr. Dover confronts Loki


 

The Dover interior lighting plan


 

The exterior location for the Dover House worked well but its interior wasn’t right for the scripted scenes. As often happens when there is exterior and interior work to shoot in the same house, it made more practical sense for us to shoot the interior elsewhere. Splitting the one set would allow for lighting to be rigged for the interior work and be held in place whilst we were shooting our exteriors. This would not only provide more weather cover but also allow us to move from exterior to interior without waiting for the set to be lit.

This sketch of the lighting for the interior location was one that took account not only of the scenes that were planned there but also the weather and time of day. Given our schedule and the winter hours, there was no guarantee of having daylight when we came to this set so I needed to light from scratch. The scene as pictured above was basically lit using the 4 x 6K Par HMIs outside the front room bay window. To facilitate ease of use we built a platform 4’ below the window level on which to place our lamps. Outside the platform (and not marked on this drawing) we secured two 20’ x 20’ Ultrabounce reflectors, angled over at 45º. Not only did this bounce source provide a substitute for the natural daylight but it also acted as a cut to any sunlight that might affect the interior lighting. By using four Par lamps, I could focus two lamps high up on the Ultrabounce, whilst evenly flooding the entire reflector with the other two lamps. Using the top of the window as a cut, I could in this way create some fall off of the light from underneath the window to the far side of the room. Again, gel frames were made to fit all the windows, so that we could adjust our diffusion between a Hampshire and a 251 depending on the camera angle. I will usually use a lighter diffusion in the background so as to allow more light to ‘wrap’ a character from the back of a shot, whilst the heavier diffusion softens the camera side. To soften the light towards the camera I might also use a separate 4’ x 4’ frame inside a window and close to the camera angle.

To the back of the house we also built a platform to extend the existing decking, so that we could more easily light through the windows on that side. Here we used 4K HMI Pars as the scene we were to shoot there was to play as later in the day and that action took place closer to the windows.

THE BACKYARD CHASE

e Backyard Chase lighting plan


 

The lighting for the backyard chase sequence was developed in the same way as all our night work. Denis and I had spent many hours walking through this sequence by ourselves and also with our storyboard artist, 1st AD and Patrice. From these discussions, I made a map of the location and the basic angles from which the camera would see the set. This gave me plenty of time to consider the placement and style of the ‘in camera’ practical sources and the ‘film’ lamps I would need to wash some trees in the back of a shot or rake a foreground. We used Nook lights to stand in for motion-controlled security lamps that reveal the barking dog and we used a variety of household bulbs to accent a door or the inside of a window. There may appear to be a lot of lighting on this diagram, but the sequence was shot at a line down from 1.4, as my assistant, Andy Harris, who had to keep focus can attest to.

The barking dog


 

The lighting for that direction


 

The two 300-watt security lights became the two nook lights, as can be seen in the overall plan.

Loki on the move


 

The reverse lighting plan


 

I made these sketches early in prep, when I had time to walk through all of our neighborhood sets by myself. They are obviously very rough, but I find they are invaluable when pre-production becomes tech scouts and an increasing variety of decisions have to be made, many of which have little to do with lighting. Besides which, I will always give my drawings and location plans to the location department in time for them to make sure we have the permissions that make any of what I am proposing to do even possible.
